stories.headline: Colorado U.S. Senate debate: Hickenlooper, Baisley face off on 9NEWS
stories.summary:
9NEWS is hosting a U.S. Senate debate Wednesday evening featuring Sen. John Hickenlooper and state Sen. Baisley, ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

The debate gives Colorado voters a direct comparison of the two candidates as ballots are being returned across the state. The Colorado Sun's Jesse Paul and Noticias Univision Colorado's Rafael Contreras moderated a separate debate held at Colorado State University in Fort Collins.

The Senate race is one of several statewide contests on the November ballot, which also carries a record-tying 14 statewide measures.

stories.headline: Millions spent in race for Colorado's 'last purple' Senate district
stories.summary:
A legislative contest in Southern Colorado has drawn more than $2.1 million in spending, most of it from outside groups, according to the latest campaign finance reports. The Senate District 3 race, based in Pueblo, is the most expensive Senate race in the state by far.

The Senate Majority Fund, which backs Republicans, has spent $980,000 to support Republican Dana Charles. All Together Colorado, which supports Democrats, has spent $858,000, about $723,000 of it to oppose Charles and about $134,000 to back Democrat Aaron Gutierrez.

Candidate fundraising has been close. Gutierrez had raised more than $126,000 against Charles' $120,000 through Sept. 30, while Charles had about $61,000 on hand to Gutierrez's $52,000. Spending across three competitive Senate races is nearing $5 million, and the outcome could shape control of the state Capitol and which major policies advance next year.

stories.headline: Colorado election office probes 'deepfake' video targeting state senator
stories.summary:
The first campaign finance complaint in Colorado over an AI-generated "deepfake" video is headed for a hearing with the Secretary of State's Elections Division. Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat, filed the complaint in August.

The video, from the Independence Institute, depicts an AI-generated Kipp as a grocery cashier who refuses to give a customer change, a metaphor for her support of Proposition NN. The measure would let the state keep and spend revenue otherwise refunded under the Taxpayer's Bill of Rights, with an estimated $4.6 billion going to public education over 10 years. The video acknowledges near its end that it is AI-generated but carries no disclaimer.

The Independence Institute called Kipp "thin-skinned" and argues the video is satire or parody, which is exempt under a 2024 law, House Bill 24-1147, that requires disclosure on deepfakes of candidates and allows civil penalties.

stories.headline: Untraceable conservative money floods Colorado to oppose tax ballot measures
stories.summary:
Millions of dollars from conservative groups that do not disclose donors have flowed into Colorado to oppose Amendment 87 and Proposition NN. Amendment 87 would impose a graduated income tax on those earning above about $500,000, raising an estimated $2 billion in its first full year for healthcare, education and childcare.

Proposition NN would eliminate potentially billions in Taxpayer's Bill of Rights refunds and redirect the money to K-12 schools and early childhood programs for at least a decade. Four issue committees are fighting the measures, including Don't Price Us Out, Brighter Colorado and Americans for Prosperity Colorado.

Don't Price Us Out took in $760,000 on Sept. 29 from the American Prosperity Coalition, registered to a Texas shipping store, and $300,000 from Ready Colorado. It spent more than $800,000 on ads in late September. Brighter Colorado had raised nearly $3 million, including $1.75 million from Common Sense America.

stories.headline: Cavender's Boot City opens second Denver-area store at Colorado Mills
stories.summary:
Western retailer Cavender's Boot City has opened a store at the Colorado Mills shopping center in Lakewood. The location is larger than 15,000 square feet and is the brand's second in the Denver area.

The company opened a Westminster store in April, which Byron Norton, vice president of stores, said is performing well. Cavender's aims to open 30 stores next year.

stories.headline: Metro district near DIA issues $203.3M in bonds for hotels, retail and PepsiCo expansion
stories.summary:
A metro district near Denver International Airport has issued $203.3 million in bonds to fund infrastructure for a major development. The money will support hotels, retail and expansion of PepsiCo facilities in the area.

The development envisions another major bottling plant along with hotels, adding to commercial growth around the airport.

stories.headline: Judge appoints receiver for X Denver apartments after owners fail to appear
stories.summary:
Judge Heidi Kutcher appointed distressed real estate firm Trigild as receiver for the 450-unit X Denver apartment complex at 3100 Inca St., north of Coors Field. She acted Friday after no one from X Denver appeared at the hearing or responded to the lawsuit.

Mack Real Estate Group of New York sued last month, saying X Denver has been in default on a $170 million loan since early 2025. The judge waited more than a month to let the owners respond.

Trigild can now run the building, advertise it for sale and eventually ask the court to approve a sale. The property's assessed value is $93.1 million, about 55% of the loan. Its original developer, The X Co., said in 2024 it was no longer affiliated, and current ownership is unclear.

stories.headline: Demolition begins in LoHi for roughly 300-unit apartment project
stories.summary:
Demolition of several buildings between Speer Boulevard and 29th Avenue began last month to make way for about 300 apartments along Bryant Street in LoHi. Public records show plans for a 7-story building on both sides of the street.

Pagewest, a recently created development firm from Aspen, is behind the project. It paid $8.5 million in October 2025 for the 1.5-acre site, formerly home to retail and office buildings.

The Speer corridor has seen heavy apartment development. Kairoi Residential is building a 429-unit complex at Zuni and Speer, and Carmel Partners wants 189 units at 2800 Speer Blvd.

stories.headline: Edible Beats restaurant group expands with Pip Food + Drink and Wooden Spoon purchase
stories.summary:
Edible Beats, the group behind Linger, Root Down and El Five, is expanding after a quiet few years. Founder Justin Cucci said the company bought Wooden Spoon Cafe & Bakery in Highland earlier this year from its departing owners.

Pip Food + Drink is set to open in five to seven weeks on the ground floor of 2930 Umatilla St., in the same building as El Five. It will be the group's first new restaurant since it sold Ophelia's Electric Soapbox in 2024.

The company is now employee-owned through an ESOP, and Cucci said the new moves are strategic growth meant to grow the ESOP. He called Linger and Root Down the anchors of the company.

stories.headline: Broncos hire Angel City FC finance executive as CFO
stories.summary: The Denver Broncos have named a new chief financial officer with sports and entertainment development experience, hiring from Angel City FC. The hire comes as the team works toward a proposed 2031 opening for a new stadium.

stories.headline: Rain and cooler temperatures arrive after record warm start to October
stories.summary:
Rain and cooler weather are headed for Colorado this week after Denver on Monday marked a record 11th straight day of 80 degrees or warmer in October. Tuesday is forecast to be partly sunny with a high of 65, with rain moving in Tuesday night.

Wednesday has a 70% chance of precipitation during the day and up to 90% at night, with highs in the upper 40s, nearly 20 degrees below normal. Thursday stays wet with a high of 54 and a low near 34.

Snow is possible above 7,000 feet, which could make mountain passes slick. A freeze watch is in effect for the San Luis Valley. Sun returns Friday with highs in the 60s, climbing to the mid-70s over the weekend.

stories.headline: Howelsen Hill in Steamboat Springs to offer free skiing on Sundays again
stories.summary:
Howelsen Hill Ski Area, Colorado's oldest continuously operating ski area, will again offer free skiing on Sundays this winter. The season is scheduled to run from Nov. 28 through March 28, conditions permitting.

Adult lift tickets are typically $55, and season passes range from $260 to $505. No reservation is needed for Sunday skiing; visitors pick up a ticket at the ticket office. Participants can show their ticket at Mountain Tap Brewery from 2 to 5 p.m. for a free beer or popcorn.

Blackout dates may apply because of snow conditions, events or training. Howelsen Hill opened in 1915, has about 50 skiable acres and has produced close to 100 winter Olympians. The city of Steamboat Springs owns and operates it.

weather.notable: About 13 degrees below the average high for this time of year.

topStory.headline: Federal Agents Search Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington Home as Investigators Subpoena Relatives in Immigration Probe
topStory.summary:
Homeland Security Investigations agents executed a court-authorized search warrant at Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington residence on Monday, October 12, according to reports, as part of a federal investigation into possible fraud and false statements in immigration paperwork. Investigators also issued subpoenas to some of her relatives. The Minnesota Democrat, 44, has represented the state's 5th Congressional District since 2019. One of the sources describes the search as an FBI search, and the precise scope of the investigation remains unclear.

According to people familiar with the matter, authorities are examining Omar's family immigration history, including whether her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, provided false information or omitted details on immigration forms before becoming a US citizen. Mohamed, a Somali educator and former military officer who later worked as a taxi driver and for the US Postal Service, died in June 2020. Omar's sister, Sahra Noor, a healthcare professional and author, has reportedly received a subpoena, as has at least one other person in the family's circle. Noor did not respond to requests for comment. A grand jury subpoena is a tool for gathering evidence and does not by itself indicate that the recipient is suspected of a crime.

Omar was born in Mogadishu, Somalia, and fled with her family at age eight during the civil war. They spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before moving to the United States in the 1990s. She has repeatedly denied allegations of immigration fraud, including claims that she married her brother to help him enter the country. No public evidence has established that her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, was her brother. Omar married political consultant Tim Mynett in March 2020. His firm, E Street Group, provided services to her 2019-2020 campaign, drawing a Federal Election Commission complaint alleging improper use and reporting of campaign funds. Omar, Mynett and the campaign denied wrongdoing, and the FEC found no reason to believe funds had been converted to personal use.

The search comes amid continuing tension between the Trump administration and Democratic officials over immigration enforcement, federal authority and the Justice Department's investigative powers. In a CBS12 interview, Jody Weis, a former Chicago Police superintendent and former FBI special agent in charge, discussed the Omar search alongside a separate ICE shooting in New York City, in which an agent fired on a suspect who officials say rammed government vehicles while trying to evade arrest. The suspect survived, and New York City leaders have questioned the agent's actions.

It is not yet known whether charges will be filed against Omar or any relative, and no charges have been announced. Further developments are expected as investigators review materials seized and gather additional testimony through subpoenas. The case is likely to remain politically charged given Omar's prominence and the broader dispute over federal immigration enforcement.
